items.stem: State what is meant by the term "impact".
items.answer: A direct effect of a digital system on people or communities, such as a change in how they work, learn or communicate
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a direct effect of a digital system on people or communities, such as a change in how they work, learn or communicate. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a digital system and a digital device.
items.answer: A device is a single piece of hardware (e.g. a smartphone); a digital system is the wider set of interacting hardware, software, data, networks and people that the device is part of (e.g. a mobile-money network such as M-Pesa).
items.markingKey: A device is a single piece of hardware (e.g. a smartphone); a digital system is the wider set of interacting hardware, software, data, networks and people that the device is part of (e.g. a mobile-money network such as M-Pesa). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "A digital technology has the same effect wherever it is used." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Impacts depend on context – political, economic, cultural – and on who uses it; social media helped organise protests in the Arab Spring but has also been used by governments for surveillance and propaganda.
items.markingKey: Impacts depend on context – political, economic, cultural – and on who uses it; social media helped organise protests in the Arab Spring but has also been used by governments for surveillance and propaganda. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Digital technologies are neither good nor bad; nor are they neutral."
— Melvin Kranzberg, historian of technology, first law of technology (1986)

Explain what the source suggests about how Digital Society students should study technology.
items.answer: The source suggests technologies have real effects (they are not neutral) but those effects depend on context and use, so students should analyse specific impacts on specific people rather than labelling a technology simply good or bad.
items.markingKey: The source suggests technologies have real effects (they are not neutral) but those effects depend on context and use, so students should analyse specific impacts on specific people rather than labelling a technology simply good or bad. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: With reference to India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI), explain how it illustrates the impact of a digital system on everyday life.
items.answer: UPI, launched in 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India, lets users pay instantly by scanning QR codes; it processes billions of transactions each month. Street vendors and large retailers alike accept instant payments, which reduces cash use and creates digital transaction records with implications for tax, credit and privacy.
items.markingKey: Context (UPI, launched in 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India, lets users pay instantly by scanning QR codes; it processes billions of transactions each month.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: street vendors and large retailers alike accept instant payments, which reduces cash use and creates digital transaction records with implications for tax, credit and privacy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the impact of a digital system on everyday life.

items.stem: Using one digital system you have studied, analyse its impacts on two different stakeholders and discuss one implication for the wider society.
items.answer: Choose a specific system (e.g. M-Pesa, UPI, a ride-hailing platform); identify two stakeholders (e.g. users and small traders, or drivers and the platform); analyse a specific impact for each with evidence; then discuss one broader implication (e.g. financial inclusion, data concentration). Reward specific detail and balance.
items.markingKey: Choose a specific system (e.g. M-Pesa, UPI, a ride-hailing platform); identify two stakeholders (e.g. users and small traders, or drivers and the platform); analyse a specific impact for each with evidence; then discuss one broader implication (e.g. financial inclusion, data concentration). Reward specific detail and balance.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "digital system"?
options: Checking whether a claim is supported by other independent and reliable sources
The study of how digital systems and technologies interact with people, communities and societies, and the impacts and implications of those interactions
A clear, specific statement of what an inquiry will investigate about a digital system and its impacts on people and communities
A set of interacting components – hardware, software, data, networks and people – that processes information in digital (binary) form to achieve a purpose
items.answer: A set of interacting components – hardware, software, data, networks and people – that processes information in digital (binary) form to achieve a purpose
items.markingKey: D. "digital system" is a set of interacting components – hardware, software, data, networks and people – that processes information in digital (binary) form to achieve a purpose.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Digital Society studies people and communities as well as technologies.
items.answer: Digital systems only have meaning through how people design, use and are affected by them; the same technology (e.g. WhatsApp) can strengthen family ties in one context and spread rumours that lead to violence in another, so impacts depend on people, values and contexts, not the device alone.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Digital systems only have meaning through how people design, use and are affected by them; the same technology (e.g. WhatsApp) can strengthen family ties in one context and spread rumours that lead to violence in another, so impacts depend on people, values and contexts, not the device alone. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which M-Pesa in Kenya shows how a digital system interacts with people and communities.
items.answer: Safaricom launched the M-Pesa mobile-money service in 2007, letting people send and store money by SMS on basic phones; it is now used by most Kenyan adults. It combines phones, the mobile network, agents and user trust to give unbanked people access to payments, changing household finance and small business in a way a single device could not.
items.markingKey: Context (Safaricom launched the M-Pesa mobile-money service in 2007, letting people send and store money by SMS on basic phones; it is now used by most Kenyan adults.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it combines phones, the mobile network, agents and user trust to give unbanked people access to payments, changing household finance and small business in a way a single device could not. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how a digital system interacts with people and communities.

items.stem: "Digital Society is mainly a course about learning to program computers." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Digital Society focuses on the impacts and implications of digital systems for people and communities; technical content (data, algorithms, networks) is studied so that its social effects can be analysed, not to write code.
items.markingKey: Digital Society focuses on the impacts and implications of digital systems for people and communities; technical content (data, algorithms, networks) is studied so that its social effects can be analysed, not to write code. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "The benefits of digital systems are shared equally by everyone in a society." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Benefits are widespread but unevenly distributed; who gains depends on access, skills and power, so equality of benefit is not automatic.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: basic services such as mobile money and UPI have reached people previously excluded from banking; free platforms (search, messaging) lower the cost of information for all. Arguments against: access, skills and affordability differ by income, gender, age and location; platform owners capture much of the value and data; some groups bear the harms (surveillance, misinformation, job loss). Supported judgement: Benefits are widespread but unevenly distributed; who gains depends on access, skills and power, so equality of benefit is not automatic. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The inquiry stage in which students communicate their findings to an audience, for example in a multimedia presentation"?
items.answer: sharing
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of sharing.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the inquiry process is described as a cycle rather than a straight line.
items.answer: Findings while investigating often raise new questions, which send students back to explore or refocus, and reflection can change how findings are shared; so the stages repeat and feed into each other rather than happening once in order.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Findings while investigating often raise new questions, which send students back to explore or refocus, and reflection can change how findings are shared; so the stages repeat and feed into each other rather than happening once in order. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an inquiry focus and a broad topic.
items.answer: A broad topic names a general area (e.g. "AI in schools"); an inquiry focus states a specific system, context and impact to investigate (e.g. "How has an AI essay-feedback tool changed writing practices at one school in Lisbon?").
items.markingKey: A broad topic names a general area (e.g. "AI in schools"); an inquiry focus states a specific system, context and impact to investigate (e.g. "How has an AI essay-feedback tool changed writing practices at one school in Lisbon?"). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using an inquiry into Wikipedia's coverage of women scientists as an example, explain how reflecting and sharing can lead to action.
items.answer: Studies have found that a minority of English Wikipedia biographies are about women; projects such as edit-a-thons and Women in Red have tried to close the gap. Reflecting on why the gap exists (editor demographics, notability rules) leads to sharing findings that may encourage interventions such as edit-a-thons.
items.markingKey: Context (Studies have found that a minority of English Wikipedia biographies are about women; projects such as edit-a-thons and Women in Red have tried to close the gap.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: reflecting on why the gap exists (editor demographics, notability rules) leads to sharing findings that may encourage interventions such as edit-a-thons. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how reflecting and sharing can lead to action.

items.stem: Arjun writes: "A good inquiry question should be as broad as possible so that more information can be found." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Broad questions produce general, descriptive answers; a focused question about a specific digital system and stakeholder allows depth and evaluation.
items.markingKey: Broad questions produce general, descriptive answers; a focused question about a specific digital system and stakeholder allows depth and evaluation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Data collection involving people must respect their informed consent and privacy. Anonymise interview data and do not publish identifiable images of minors."
— School research ethics guidance for the Digital Society inquiry project

Explain which stage of the inquiry process this guidance is most relevant to and why.
items.answer: Mainly investigating (when collecting primary data from people) and reflecting (considering ethics); it ensures research is ethical and protects participants, which also affects how findings can be shared.
items.markingKey: Mainly investigating (when collecting primary data from people) and reflecting (considering ethics); it ensures research is ethical and protects participants, which also affects how findings can be shared. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A student wants to investigate "social media and politics". Using the inquiry process, explain how they should refine this topic into a focused inquiry and plan their investigation.
items.answer: Exploring: choose a specific system and context (e.g. TikTok political content in the 2024 Indonesian election) and write a guiding question; investigating: identify a range of sources (platform reports, news, academic studies, interviews) and perspectives (voters, campaigners, regulators); reflecting: plan to assess bias, limitations and ethics; sharing: choose a format and audience. Reward a specific focus and a coherent plan.
items.markingKey: Exploring: choose a specific system and context (e.g. TikTok political content in the 2024 Indonesian election) and write a guiding question; investigating: identify a range of sources (platform reports, news, academic studies, interviews) and perspectives (voters, campaigners, regulators); reflecting: plan to assess bias, limitations and ethics; sharing: choose a format and audience. Reward a specific focus and a coherent plan.

items.stem: "A personal, primary investigation is always more valuable than secondary sources in a Digital Society inquiry." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Primary evidence adds originality and local depth, but it is most valuable when combined with credible secondary sources that provide scale and context.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: primary data (interviews, surveys) can capture local impacts not reported elsewhere; it gives direct insight into stakeholder perspectives. Arguments against: small samples may not be representative; secondary sources (reports, academic studies) give scale and context; primary research raises ethical and time constraints. Supported judgement: Primary evidence adds originality and local depth, but it is most valuable when combined with credible secondary sources that provide scale and context. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: Explain why reflecting is an important stage of the inquiry process.
items.answer: Reflection lets students recognise gaps or bias in their evidence, consider ethical issues (e.g. consent of interviewees), and judge the significance of findings, which turns a description into a critical, balanced conclusion.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Reflection lets students recognise gaps or bias in their evidence, consider ethical issues (e.g. consent of interviewees), and judge the significance of findings, which turns a description into a critical, balanced conclusion. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why narrowing an inquiry focus improves the quality of an investigation.
items.answer: A narrow focus (one system, one place, one group) lets students find specific evidence, compare perspectives in depth and evaluate impacts precisely, whereas a broad topic (e.g. "social media") leads to generalisations and descriptive answers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A narrow focus (one system, one place, one group) lets students find specific evidence, compare perspectives in depth and evaluate impacts precisely, whereas a broad topic (e.g. "social media") leads to generalisations and descriptive answers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between investigating and exploring.
items.answer: Exploring is about identifying a real-world example and forming a focus and questions; investigating is about systematically gathering and analysing evidence from different sources and perspectives to answer them.
items.markingKey: Exploring is about identifying a real-world example and forming a focus and questions; investigating is about systematically gathering and analysing evidence from different sources and perspectives to answer them. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which an inquiry into Wikipedia's coverage of women scientists shows how reflecting and sharing can lead to action.
items.answer: Studies have found that a minority of English Wikipedia biographies are about women; projects such as edit-a-thons and Women in Red have tried to close the gap. Reflecting on why the gap exists (editor demographics, notability rules) leads to sharing findings that may encourage interventions such as edit-a-thons.
items.markingKey: Context (Studies have found that a minority of English Wikipedia biographies are about women; projects such as edit-a-thons and Women in Red have tried to close the gap.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: reflecting on why the gap exists (editor demographics, notability rules) leads to sharing findings that may encourage interventions such as edit-a-thons. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how reflecting and sharing can lead to action.

items.stem: "The most important stage of the inquiry process is sharing findings with an audience." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Sharing gives an inquiry impact, but its value depends on rigorous investigation and honest reflection earlier in the cycle.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: communication makes the inquiry useful to others and may prompt action; the IA is assessed through a presentation. Arguments against: sharing weak or biased findings is of little value; investigation and reflection determine the quality of what is shared. Supported judgement: Sharing gives an inquiry impact, but its value depends on rigorous investigation and honest reflection earlier in the cycle. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Our guiding question changed three times. We began with 'Is TikTok bad for teenagers?', which was impossible to answer. We ended with 'How has TikTok's For You feed changed how students at our school discover music?' – and then we could actually gather evidence."
— Reflection by an IB Digital Society student, school blog, 2024

With reference to the source, explain why the student changed their guiding question.
items.answer: The first question was too broad and value-laden to answer with evidence; the final question names a specific system (the For You feed), group (students at one school) and impact (music discovery), so evidence could be collected and evaluated.
items.markingKey: The first question was too broad and value-laden to answer with evidence; the final question names a specific system (the For You feed), group (students at one school) and impact (music discovery), so evidence could be collected and evaluated. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: In the CRAAP test for evaluating sources, what does the second "A" stand for?
items.answer: Accuracy
items.markingKey: B. CRAAP = Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

items.stem: A student claims: "If a website looks professional and has a .org address, its claims must be reliable." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Design and domain names say little about reliability; anyone can register a .org domain, so authority, evidence, purpose and corroboration must be checked.
items.markingKey: Design and domain names say little about reliability; anyone can register a .org domain, so authority, evidence, purpose and corroboration must be checked. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a source can be useful even if it is biased.
items.answer: A biased source still reveals the perspective, interests and arguments of a stakeholder (e.g. a tech company blog shows how the firm justifies its product), which is valuable evidence when compared with other perspectives, as long as its limitations are recognised. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A biased source still reveals the perspective, interests and arguments of a stakeholder (e.g. a tech company blog shows how the firm justifies its product), which is valuable evidence when compared with other perspectives, as long as its limitations are recognised. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Our app reduced screen time by 37% among teenage users in a 4-week trial."
— Press release from the company that makes the screen-time app, 2024

Identify two questions you would ask to evaluate the reliability of this claim.
items.answer: For example: Who conducted and funded the trial (the company itself – conflict of interest)? How many participants were there and how were they chosen? Was there a control group? Is the data or method published and independently verified? Over what period was it measured?
items.markingKey: For example: Who conducted and funded the trial (the company itself – conflict of interest)? How many participants were there and how were they chosen? Was there a control group? Is the data or method published and independently verified? Over what period was it measured? Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using Meta's transparency reports as an example, explain the value and limitations of primary sources.
items.answer: Meta regularly publishes Community Standards Enforcement Reports with figures on content removed and the share found by its own systems before users reported it. They provide first-hand data at a scale no outsider could collect, but they are produced by the company itself and use its own definitions, so their figures should be corroborated by independent research.
items.markingKey: Context (Meta regularly publishes Community Standards Enforcement Reports with figures on content removed and the share found by its own systems before users reported it.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: they provide first-hand data at a scale no outsider could collect, but they are produced by the company itself and use its own definitions, so their figures should be corroborated by independent research. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the value and limitations of primary sources.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Professional journalism is always more reliable than social media as a source for a Digital Society inquiry."
items.answer: Professional journalism is usually more reliable, but reliability must be judged source by source; social media can be valuable primary evidence if verified.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: journalists follow editorial standards, fact-checking and corrections; named authors and organisations can be held accountable. Arguments against: social media can provide first-hand evidence from places journalists cannot reach (e.g. protests); news organisations can also have bias and commercial pressures; reliability depends on the specific source, not the medium. Supported judgement: Professional journalism is usually more reliable, but reliability must be judged source by source; social media can be valuable primary evidence if verified.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "perspective"?
options: The cycle of exploring, investigating, reflecting and sharing that Digital Society students use to study real-world digital systems
The point of view from which a stakeholder interprets a digital system or issue, shaped by their interests, values and experience
A direct effect of a digital system on people or communities, such as a change in how they work, learn or communicate
The inquiry stage in which students communicate their findings to an audience, for example in a multimedia presentation
items.answer: The point of view from which a stakeholder interprets a digital system or issue, shaped by their interests, values and experience
items.markingKey: B. "perspective" is the point of view from which a stakeholder interprets a digital system or issue, shaped by their interests, values and experience.

items.stem: Distinguish between a secondary source and a primary source.
items.answer: A primary source is first-hand evidence (e.g. a government dataset, an interview with a gig worker); a secondary source interprets or analyses such evidence (e.g. a journalist's article summarising several studies).
items.markingKey: A primary source is first-hand evidence (e.g. a government dataset, an interview with a gig worker); a secondary source interprets or analyses such evidence (e.g. a journalist's article summarising several studies). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "A source with a clear perspective is useless for an inquiry." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Perspective-driven sources show how stakeholders see an issue; they are useful if their purpose is identified and they are compared with other sources.
items.markingKey: Perspective-driven sources show how stakeholders see an issue; they are useful if their purpose is identified and they are compared with other sources. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "investigating".
items.answer: The inquiry stage in which students gather, analyse and evaluate sources and evidence from different perspectives
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the inquiry stage in which students gather, analyse and evaluate sources and evidence from different perspectives. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.answer: Collecting sources is only part of investigating; students must also analyse and evaluate them, reflect on limitations and ethics, and share findings with an audience.

items.stem: Explain why claims about digital technology should be corroborated.
items.answer: Claims spread quickly online and may be exaggerated, out of context or deliberately false; checking them against independent, reliable sources reduces the risk of building an argument on misinformation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why it is useful to distinguish between impacts and implications when studying a digital system.
items.answer: Impacts are immediate effects (e.g. video calls replace face-to-face lessons) while implications are wider, longer-term consequences (e.g. deepening inequality for students without devices); separating them helps an inquiry move from description to evaluation of significance.

items.stem: Using an inquiry into food-delivery riders in Bogotá as an example, explain the importance of investigating different perspectives.
items.answer: Riders for platforms such as Rappi in Colombia have protested about pay and safety, while the platform argues that flexible work benefits riders and customers. A balanced investigation would compare rider interviews, company statements and government data, rather than relying on one perspective, before reaching a conclusion.
items.markingKey: Context (Riders for platforms such as Rappi in Colombia have protested about pay and safety, while the platform argues that flexible work benefits riders and customers.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to the move to online schooling during COVID-19, explain how it illustrates how impacts differ between stakeholders.
items.answer: In 2020 school closures affected over 1.5 billion learners worldwide (UNESCO), and many systems moved lessons to video-conferencing and learning platforms. Students with devices and broadband continued learning, while those without access fell behind, showing that the same digital system had unequal impacts and long-term implications for educational inequality.

Read the source below.

"For many of our members, the WhatsApp group is the village square: births, funerals and job offers are shared there first. But when a false rumour about child kidnappers spread in 2018, the same groups carried it to thousands of phones within hours."
— Community worker in Maharashtra, India, interviewed for a 2019 report on messaging apps

With reference to the source, explain one positive and one negative impact of messaging apps on communities.
items.answer: Positive: groups act as a community hub, spreading news of births, funerals and jobs quickly. Negative: the same speed and reach spread a false kidnapping rumour widely in hours (such rumours were linked to mob attacks in India in 2018).

Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"A lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes."
— Saying commonly misattributed to Mark Twain; versions date back to the 18th century

Explain how this source itself illustrates a problem with evaluating claims.
items.answer: The quotation is widely shared with a false attribution to Twain; it shows how easily claims (even about sources) are repeated without checking, so attribution and origin must be verified.
items.markingKey: The quotation is widely shared with a false attribution to Twain; it shows how easily claims (even about sources) are repeated without checking, so attribution and origin must be verified. items.stem: Briefly describe an inquiry into food-delivery riders in Bogotá and explain what it reveals about the importance of investigating different perspectives.
items.answer: Riders for platforms such as Rappi in Colombia have protested about pay and safety, while the platform argues that flexible work benefits riders and customers. A balanced investigation would compare rider interviews, company statements and government data, rather than relying on one perspective, before reaching a conclusion.
items.markingKey: Context (Riders for platforms such as Rappi in Colombia have protested about pay and safety, while the platform argues that flexible work benefits riders and customers.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a balanced investigation would compare rider interviews, company statements and government data, rather than relying on one perspective, before reaching a conclusion. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the importance of investigating different perspectives.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The benefits of digital systems are shared equally by everyone in a society."
items.answer: Benefits are widespread but unevenly distributed; who gains depends on access, skills and power, so equality of benefit is not automatic.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: basic services such as mobile money and UPI have reached people previously excluded from banking; free platforms (search, messaging) lower the cost of information for all. Arguments against: access, skills and affordability differ by income, gender, age and location; platform owners capture much of the value and data; some groups bear the harms (surveillance, misinformation, job loss). Supported judgement: Benefits are widespread but unevenly distributed; who gains depends on access, skills and power, so equality of benefit is not automatic.

items.stem: Two sources disagree about whether a city's smart-camera system has reduced crime: a council press release and a report by a civil liberties group. Explain how you would evaluate these sources and reach a conclusion.
items.answer: Consider origin, purpose and possible bias of each (council promoting its policy; NGO campaigning on privacy); examine evidence quality (data, time period, methods, comparison areas); look for independent corroboration (police statistics, academic studies); recognise each perspective's value; reach a qualified conclusion based on the strongest evidence.
items.markingKey: Consider origin, purpose and possible bias of each (council promoting its policy; NGO campaigning on privacy); examine evidence quality (data, time period, methods, comparison areas); look for independent corroboration (police statistics, academic studies); recognise each perspective's value; reach a qualified conclusion based on the strongest evidence.

items.stem: "A personal, primary investigation is always more valuable than secondary sources in a Digital Society inquiry." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Primary evidence adds originality and local depth, but it is most valuable when combined with credible secondary sources that provide scale and context.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: primary data (interviews, surveys) can capture local impacts not reported elsewhere; it gives direct insight into stakeholder perspectives. Arguments against: small samples may not be representative; secondary sources (reports, academic studies) give scale and context; primary research raises ethical and time constraints. Supported judgement: Primary evidence adds originality and local depth, but it is most valuable when combined with credible secondary sources that provide scale and context. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: "Studying the impacts of a digital system is more important than understanding how it works." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Both are needed: understanding how a system works explains its impacts, and impacts give that knowledge its significance.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Digital Society is concerned with consequences for people and communities; stakeholders and policymakers need to judge impacts to act. Arguments against: without understanding how a system works (data, algorithms) students cannot explain why impacts occur; technical misunderstandings lead to weak interventions. Supported judgement: Both are needed: understanding how a system works explains its impacts, and impacts give that knowledge its significance. items.stem: Which of the following is the IB Digital Society internal assessment?
options: An oral examination on a novel
An inquiry project presented as a multimedia presentation
items.answer: An inquiry project presented as a multimedia presentation
items.markingKey: C. The IA is an inquiry into a real-world digital system shared as a multimedia presentation.

items.stem: Which of the following is one of the seven key concepts of the IB Digital Society course?
items.answer: Expression
items.markingKey: C. The concepts are change, expression, identity, power, space, systems, and values and ethics.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A statement presented as true that needs to be supported by evidence and reasoning"?
items.answer: claim
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of claim.

items.stem: Explain the difference between exploring and investigating.
items.answer: Exploring is about identifying a real-world example and forming a focus and questions; investigating is about systematically gathering and analysing evidence from different sources and perspectives to answer them.
items.markingKey: Exploring is about identifying a real-world example and forming a focus and questions; investigating is about systematically gathering and analysing evidence from different sources and perspectives to answer them. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between an implication and an impact.
items.answer: An impact is a direct effect of a digital system (e.g. faster banking through an app); an implication is a broader or longer-term consequence that follows (e.g. branch closures that exclude elderly people without smartphones).
items.markingKey: An impact is a direct effect of a digital system (e.g. faster banking through an app); an implication is a broader or longer-term consequence that follows (e.g. branch closures that exclude elderly people without smartphones). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a claim and evidence.
items.answer: A claim is an assertion that something is true (e.g. "smartphones harm teenagers' sleep"); evidence is the data or testimony used to support or challenge it (e.g. results of a sleep study).
items.markingKey: A claim is an assertion that something is true (e.g. "smartphones harm teenagers' sleep"); evidence is the data or testimony used to support or challenge it (e.g. results of a sleep study). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A good inquiry question should be as broad as possible so that more information can be found." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Broad questions produce general, descriptive answers; a focused question about a specific digital system and stakeholder allows depth and evaluation.
items.markingKey: Broad questions produce general, descriptive answers; a focused question about a specific digital system and stakeholder allows depth and evaluation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Freya writes: "A digital technology has the same effect wherever it is used." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Impacts depend on context – political, economic, cultural – and on who uses it; social media helped organise protests in the Arab Spring but has also been used by governments for surveillance and propaganda.
items.markingKey: Impacts depend on context – political, economic, cultural – and on who uses it; social media helped organise protests in the Arab Spring but has also been used by governments for surveillance and propaganda. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the date of a source matters when evaluating claims about digital technology.
items.answer: Digital systems, laws and usage change rapidly (e.g. platform policies, AI capabilities), so an older source may describe a situation that no longer applies; currency affects relevance and accuracy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Digital systems, laws and usage change rapidly (e.g. platform policies, AI capabilities), so an older source may describe a situation that no longer applies; currency affects relevance and accuracy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe an inquiry into Wikipedia's coverage of women scientists and explain what it reveals about how reflecting and sharing can lead to action.
items.answer: Studies have found that a minority of English Wikipedia biographies are about women; projects such as edit-a-thons and Women in Red have tried to close the gap. Reflecting on why the gap exists (editor demographics, notability rules) leads to sharing findings that may encourage interventions such as edit-a-thons.
items.markingKey: Context (Studies have found that a minority of English Wikipedia biographies are about women; projects such as edit-a-thons and Women in Red have tried to close the gap.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: reflecting on why the gap exists (editor demographics, notability rules) leads to sharing findings that may encourage interventions such as edit-a-thons. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how reflecting and sharing can lead to action.

items.stem: Briefly describe India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and explain what it reveals about the impact of a digital system on everyday life.
items.answer: UPI, launched in 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India, lets users pay instantly by scanning QR codes; it processes billions of transactions each month. Street vendors and large retailers alike accept instant payments, which reduces cash use and creates digital transaction records with implications for tax, credit and privacy.
items.markingKey: Context (UPI, launched in 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India, lets users pay instantly by scanning QR codes; it processes billions of transactions each month.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: street vendors and large retailers alike accept instant payments, which reduces cash use and creates digital transaction records with implications for tax, credit and privacy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the impact of a digital system on everyday life.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the "Pope in a puffer jacket" image (2023) shows the need to verify visual sources.
items.answer: In March 2023 an AI-generated image of Pope Francis in a white puffer jacket, made with Midjourney, spread widely and was believed by many to be a real photograph. Even realistic images can be synthetic, so students should check the origin of an image (reverse image search, credible reporting) before using it as evidence.

items.stem: Using the move to online schooling during COVID-19 as an example, explain how impacts differ between stakeholders.
items.answer: In 2020 school closures affected over 1.5 billion learners worldwide (UNESCO), and many systems moved lessons to video-conferencing and learning platforms. Students with devices and broadband continued learning, while those without access fell behind, showing that the same digital system had unequal impacts and long-term implications for educational inequality.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Meta's transparency reports shows the value and limitations of primary sources.
items.answer: Meta regularly publishes Community Standards Enforcement Reports with figures on content removed and the share found by its own systems before users reported it. They provide first-hand data at a scale no outsider could collect, but they are produced by the company itself and use its own definitions, so their figures should be corroborated by independent research.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Studying the impacts of a digital system is more important than understanding how it works."
items.answer: Both are needed: understanding how a system works explains its impacts, and impacts give that knowledge its significance.

Supported judgement: Both are needed: understanding how a system works explains its impacts, and impacts give that knowledge its significance.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that professional journalism is always more reliable than social media as a source for a Digital Society inquiry.
items.answer: Professional journalism is usually more reliable, but reliability must be judged source by source; social media can be valuable primary evidence if verified.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: journalists follow editorial standards, fact-checking and corrections; named authors and organisations can be held accountable. Arguments against: social media can provide first-hand evidence from places journalists cannot reach (e.g. protests); news organisations can also have bias and commercial pressures; reliability depends on the specific source, not the medium. Supported judgement: Professional journalism is usually more reliable, but reliability must be judged source by source; social media can be valuable primary evidence if verified. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The most important stage of the inquiry process is sharing findings with an audience."
items.answer: Sharing gives an inquiry impact, but its value depends on rigorous investigation and honest reflection earlier in the cycle.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: communication makes the inquiry useful to others and may prompt action; the IA is assessed through a presentation. Arguments against: sharing weak or biased findings is of little value; investigation and reflection determine the quality of what is shared.
